proyectos.intro: Each one told the same way: what the problem was, what I built, and what changed afterwards.

items.titular: A welding workshop in rural Spain, with local SEO and photo quotes
items.resumen: A complete website for a welding and metalwork shop in Guardo, rural Spain. Built in full before the client ever saw it, and sold by presenting it finished.
items.problema: A new workshop in a rural area with no website and its whole presence on Instagram. Anyone searching for a welder nearby could not find it, and the work went to the city instead.
items.solucion: A single-page site covering its four service lines, coverage area, a floating WhatsApp button and a quote form with photo attachment. Local SEO with structured data so it surfaces in nearby searches. Built in stealth, unindexed, so it could be handed over finished.
items.resultado: Measured on mobile against a production build: 98-99 for performance, and 100 for accessibility, best practices and SEO. It is live; the custom domain and a copy pass with the client are still pending.
items.imagenAlt: Homepage of the AVP_INOX site, headline reading Soldadura y carpintería metálica over a brushed steel surface

items.titular: A bar was spending its only day off each week sorting invoices
items.resumen: An n8n workflow that collects invoices, files them in Google Drive and every quarter sends them, grouped, to the accountant. Nobody has to remember.
items.problema: A bar receives invoices from a long list of suppliers: two beer distributors, the coffee one, the potato one, electricity, water, the cigarette machine, the local supermarkets. The owner spent Tuesdays, his only day off in the week, digging them out of his inbox one by one, renaming them, filing them into Drive folders and logging them in a spreadsheet. All by hand. And once a month he drove to the accountant in person with the printed stack.
items.solucion: An n8n workflow that watches the inbox and recognises suppliers from a list held in Google Sheets, so adding a new one never means touching the workflow. It reads the date off the invoice itself rather than the email, because a March invoice can arrive in April. It files the document in Drive by year and month under a consistent name, logs it, and notifies by email and Telegram. Duplicates are caught twice over: a fingerprint in the ledger, and a filename check in the folder itself. It is deliberately split into two workflows: one watches the inbox daily and files, the other handles the quarterly close. If one breaks, the other keeps running.
items.resultado: Around two hours every week, plus a morning each month at the accountant's. Close to a hundred hours a year given back, and more to the point, the only day off he had. Digital invoices file themselves, and every quarter they go to the accountant grouped, with nobody having to remember.
items.metricasNota: Estimated from the time the client spent before it was automated

items.titular: Shared calendar and tasks, with its own server and database
items.resumen: A complete application with its own server, database and account system. It started from a personal need and became the place where everything gets tested before it reaches client work.
items.problema: Coordinating a calendar, tasks and plans between two people in different time zones, one of them in China. The off-the-shelf options depend on Google services, which are not reliably reachable there.
items.solucion: Its own password and session authentication, deliberately free of external providers, precisely because access to third-party APIs cannot be guaranteed from China. A database with automated backups and scheduled credential rotation. Interface in Spanish, English and Chinese, with dates and formats resolved by the browser itself rather than hand-written lists.
items.resultado: Eleven independent modules, a versioned API and tests over the critical routes. Proof that the approach holds up for something larger than a one-page site.
